Title: Imbalance: Resampling, Weighting, Calibration VS No Intervention Strategy | by Aleksandr Golovin | Medium
2. `.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)`: This method fits the undersampler to the training data (`X_train` and `y_train`) and applies the sampling strategy to create a new, resampled dataset with balanced class distribution. So, the resulting `X_train_rus` and `y_train_rus` arrays will have fewer samples from the majority class, making the training set more balanced and less prone to overfitting on the majority class. Training with the original class distribution allows the model to learn from the natural distribution of the data, which can help it perform better in real-world scenarios. Training with a balanced class distribution can help address class imbalance issues, but may also introduce bias into the model. `model_balanced` will be trained on balanced data, which means that the positive and negative samples in the training set are roughly equal in number. This means that the training set will be used to train `calibrated_model` contains a higher number of samples from one class compared to the other(s), which reflects the true distribution of the data in the real world. **Calibration** is the process of mapping the output of a classification model to a probability score that can be interpreted as the likelihood of a sample belonging to a particular class. This code is fitting a model to training data, making predictions on test data, and then extracting the probability estimates for the positive class. 2. `y_pred = model.predict_proba(X_test)`: This line of code generates predicted probabilities for each class for the test data `X_test`. In summary, the code is fitting a models, predicting probabilities on a separate test set, and then extracting the probability estimates for the positive class. The two metrics calculated provide different aspects of the model's performance, with the ROC AUC focusing on the model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative cases, and the Brier score measuring the calibration or accuracy of the predicted probabilities. The analysis demonstrates that when dealing with imbalanced data, calibrating a model or leaving the model and data as is can result in better performance in terms of the Brier score for probability predictions using logistic regression models.

results.title: [PDF] Resampling Methods for Class Imbalance in Clinical Prediction ...
results.content: Methods and analysis: We will search MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and IEEE Xplore, plus grey-literature sources (medRxiv, arXiv, bioRxiv) for primary studies (2009 – 31 Dec 2024) that apply at least one resampling or cost-sensitive method to binary clinical prediction tasks with a minority-class prevalence <30 %. A descriptive synthesis will catalogue clinical domain, sample size, imbalance ratio, resampling technique, model type and performance metrics where≥10 studies report compatible AUCs, a random-effects mixed-effects meta-regression (logit-transformed AUC) will examine moderators including imbalance ratio, resampling class, model family and sample size. Objectives Primary objective To determine, across clinical prediction studies with binary outcomes and minority‐class prevalence < 30 %, whether applying data-level resampling or algorithm-level cost-sensitive strategies measurably improves model performance relative to training on the original imbalanced data. ; https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.05.19.25327868 doi: medRxiv preprint • Interventions: Data-level resampling (random oversampling, random undersampling, SMOTE or variants, hybrid pipelines) and algorithm-level cost-sensitive techniques (weighted losses, focal loss). Data extraction A piloted, standardised form will capture bibliometrics, clinical domain, sample size, imbalance ratio, resampling strategy, model family, performance metrics, calibration statistics, and cost-sensitive measures.

results.title: Focal Loss Demystified. I came across the term ‘Focal Loss’… | by Divakar Kapil | Escapades in Machine Learning | Medium
results.content: So, the more box proposals created for an image means that more of them will contain backgrounds rather than the objects for example say 1000 boxes are created by the detector and the number of objects to be detected is only 5. This leads to a data imbalance problem as too many background examples will bias the classifier to empasize the background in order to minimise the loss. Before we dive into the details of ‘Focal Loss’, let’s understand how two-staged detectors are able to avoid the data imbalance problem. This is a new loss function created specifically to deal with the data imbalance problem for one-staged detectors. It reshapes the cross entropy loss in such a way that it down weighs the loss assigned to well classified examples. The un-augmented cross entropy loss does the same that is it will treat the background examples as the main class to be predicted and treat the objects as noise and hence pay less attention to the loss computed on them. Even though the loss seems to be pretty insignificant, it can completely overwhelm the minority class when it is summed over a large number of easy examples. Say, the loss assigned to every well classified (easy examples) is 1 and misclassified example is 10. It is evident that when gamma=0, we get CE(pt) which assigns a small value of loss to well-classified examples. A common method to deal with the data imbalance problem employed in the cross entropy loss is to introduce a weighting factor ‘α’ which takes the values in the range 0 to 1.For notational convenience, ‘αt’ is defined similar to ‘pt’. Focal loss down weighs the easy examples and lays emphasis on the hard negative examples. By using the predicted probability ‘pt’, the loss function is able to deal with the hard and easy examples which the augmented cross entropy was unable to. 2. As ‘pt’ approaches 1, the modulating factor (1 − pt)^γ approaches 0 and the loss of the well classified examples is down weighted. For example, when ‘γ’ = 0 then focal loss becomes normal cross entropy loss.

results.title: Focal difficult-to-predict pixels dice loss for mitigating data imbalance in medical image segmentation | Request PDF
results.content: Focal difficult-to-predict pixels dice loss for mitigating data imbalance in medical image segmentation | Request PDF. Focal difficult-to-predict pixels dice loss for mitigating data imbalance in medical image segmentation. Starting from the difficulties in medical image segmentation, this paper first introduces the loss function and improvement strategies to solve the problems of sample imbalance, edge blur, false positive and false negative. Unified Focal loss: Generalising Dice and cross entropy-based losses to handle class imbalanced medical image segmentation. We evaluate our proposed loss function on five publicly available, class imbalanced medical imaging datasets: CVC-ClinicDB, Digital Retinal Images for Vessel Extraction (DRIVE), Breast Ultrasound 2017 (BUS2017), Brain Tumour Segmentation 2020 (BraTS20) and Kidney Tumour Segmentation 2019 (KiTS19). We compare our loss function performance against six Dice or cross entropy-based loss functions, across 2D binary, 3D binary and 3D multiclass segmentation tasks, demonstrating that our proposed loss function is robust to class imbalance and consistently outperforms the other loss functions. While deep learning-based approaches have achieved impressive performance in semantic segmentation, they are limited to pixel-wise settings with imbalanced-class data problems and weak boundary object segmentation in medical images. To address this problem, we investigated how loss weighting strategies work for brain structure segmentation tasks with different class imbalance situations on MR images. The results suggested that the distance map-based and the focal weightings could boost the performance of cross-entropy and Dice loss functions in class imbalanced segmentation tasks, respectively. In this review, we categorize the leading deep learning-based medical and non-medical image segmentation solutions into six main groups of deep architectural, data synthesis-based, loss function-based, sequenced models, weakly supervised, and multi-task methods and provide a comprehensive review of the contributions in each of these groups. We verify these results empirically in an extensive validation on six medical segmentation tasks and can confirm that metric-sensitive losses are superior to cross-entropy based loss functions in case of evaluation with Dice Score or Jaccard Index. We also propose to use the class re-balancing properties of the Generalized Dice overlap, a known metric for segmentation assessment, as a robust and accurate deep-learning loss function for unbalanced tasks.
